newsitem.title: USA: Europeans disappointed by G7 environment stand.
newsitem.headline: Europeans disappointed by G7 environment stand.

text.p: Under U.S. pressure, the Group of Seven industrialised nations summit ended on Sunday with a compromise on global warming that disappointed European leaders hoping to take the lead at this week's U.N. Earth Summit.

The annual G7 summit, ending a day before the U.N. meeting opens in New York, issued a communique that fell short of European Union calls for a clear target for substantial cuts in the carbon emissions that cause the "greenhouse effect".

It said the G7 wanted clear and realistic targets for carbon emission cuts but avoided the target -- a 15 percent reduction by the year 2010 -- that the EU has agreed as its position for the Earth Summit.
The special U.N. General Assembly session in New York will discuss progress in fighting global warming since the first Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro five years ago.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl shrugged when asked why the four Eurpean G7 states -- Britain, France, Germany and Italy -- could not convince their partners, the United States, Japan and Canada, to commit themselves now to tougher targets.
"Nobody can answer that question," he told journalists. "We couldn't get any more on that. The Europeans are simply further along (on environmental protection)."

European Commission President Jacques Santer said: "I am frankly disappointed that not all our partners were able here and now to take quantified commitments on the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions. We must stop the degradation of our climate. The future of the planet is at stake."

Environmental groups also criticised the compromise. Clinton had missed an opportunity to join with the Europeans "in putting the global warming negotations back on track," said Alden Meyer of the Union of Concerned Scientists.
Delegation officials said Clinton, apparently concerned about unpopular energy price hikes that any tough agreement could bring, told his partners they should not make problems for each other.

The environment dispute produced one of the few points of discord at the Denver summit of the G7, the forum of leading industrialised states that meets annually to set broad economic and political policy lines for the next year.
Kohl said the issue was the most difficult at the summit and split the rich nations' club into two blocs.

The United States accounts for almost a quarter of all greenhouse gases emitted around the world when fossil fuels like oil and coal are burned. Scientists say these emissions will lead to dangerous climate changes in the next century if unchecked.

French President Jacques Chirac, whose country's heavy use of nuclear power means it is low on greenhouse gas emissions, pulled no punches about the Americans' record. "They pollute enormously," he declared after the summit ended.
The communique said the G7 states wanted a "strong agreement" with quantified and legally-binding emission targets bbefore a U.N. conference on climate change in Kyoto in December.
It spoke of "meaningful, realistic and equitable targets" and dropped stronger references in earlier drafts about significant or substantial reductions in emission levels.
In his final news conference, Clinton said world leaders "intend to reach an agreement in Kyoto to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to respond to the problem of global warming."

British Prime Minister Tony Blair said his country would aim to cut its greenhouse gas emissions by 20 percent in 2010 compared with 1990, adding he would tell the Earth Summit that world leaders had to agree to target figures at Kyoto.
"We in Europe have put our cards on the table," he said in an implied challenge to Washington. "It's time for the special pleading to stop and for others to follow suit."

Kohl dismissed U.S. arguments against setting firm targets for pollution control now. "The Americans say they've had great economic growth in the past four years without limits and that we had limits and had poorer growth," he said. "This argument doesn't merit further consideration, but they use it."
